# External validation on real CGM data (ShanghaiT2DM)

*Generated by `scripts/validate_shanghai.py`. 107 real recordings, 17 of those patients on a sulfonylurea. The twin was **not retrained**: the published EHR row sets its prior and the particle filter personalises it from the glucose trace alone.*

## Why this matters

Every other number in this repository comes from a simulator we wrote. This one does not. ShanghaiT2DM is 109 continuous glucose recordings from people with type 2 diabetes in Shanghai, published with the labs and medication lists the twin's prior needs.

**Summary: the twin does not currently transfer to this dataset.** The detail, and our best explanation, are below. We ran this because a proof of concept measured only on its own simulator proves very little, and we are reporting the outcome rather than the intention.

**What this does and does not validate.** The cohort is Chinese, not Indian, and carries no festival calendar, no fasting days and no wearable streams. So this tests the *mechanistic twin and its glucose forecast on real physiology*. It does not validate the fasting-aware part of the system, which still rests entirely on simulation.

### CGM only

*no meal log at all - the twin sees glucose and the EHR, nothing else*

| Horizon | n forecasts | Twin RMSE | Persistence RMSE | Twin MARD | Twin Clarke A+B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 min | 18,918 | 34.5 mg/dL | 18.4 mg/dL | 19.7% | 95.6% |
| 60 min | 18,877 | 43.3 mg/dL | 30.8 mg/dL | 24.4% | 93.4% |
| 120 min | 18,795 | 52.2 mg/dL | 46.0 mg/dL | 28.4% | 91.4% |

### CGM + meal timing

*meal *times* from the diet column, with a fixed 50 g assumed per meal, since the column is free text and carries no amount*

| Horizon | n forecasts | Twin RMSE | Persistence RMSE | Twin MARD | Twin Clarke A+B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 min | 18,918 | 56.5 mg/dL | 18.4 mg/dL | 29.9% | 90.4% |
| 60 min | 18,877 | 62.9 mg/dL | 30.8 mg/dL | 34.0% | 88.2% |
| 120 min | 18,795 | 68.0 mg/dL | 46.0 mg/dL | 37.0% | 87.7% |

### Sulfonylurea-treated patients only

This project is about sulfonylurea risk, so the subgroup matters more than the average. 17 of these recordings are from patients on a sulfonylurea (gliclazide, glimepiride, gliquidone or repaglinide).

| Horizon | n forecasts | Twin RMSE | Persistence RMSE | Twin Clarke A+B |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 min | 3,385 | 31.6 mg/dL | 18.2 mg/dL | 97.5% |
| 60 min | 3,378 | 43.9 mg/dL | 30.3 mg/dL | 92.8% |
| 120 min | 3,364 | 59.5 mg/dL | 45.1 mg/dL | 90.8% |

## The result

**The twin did not beat persistence on this dataset, at any horizon.**

At 2 hours it reaches **52 mg/dL RMSE** against **46 mg/dL** for simply assuming glucose stays where it is, with 91.4% of forecasts in Clarke zones A+B (persistence: 95.5%). Our own simulator puts the twin at roughly 38 mg/dL at the same horizon, comfortably ahead of persistence there. It does not transfer.

The gap narrows with horizon — the twin is 1.9× persistence at 30 minutes and 1.14× at 2 hours — which is the signature of a model whose *dynamics* are roughly right but whose *state and parameters* are poorly initialised, rather than one whose physics is wrong.

### Why, as best we can tell

1. **The prior has never seen a real patient.** The EHR → physiology mapping in `upvaas/twin/priors.py` is a ridge regression fitted on our own synthetic generator. Applied to real Shanghai inpatients it starts every particle from the wrong place, and three days of sparse CGM is not enough for the filter to recover. This is the most likely single cause and it is entirely our doing.
2. **There is no meal log.** The dataset records diet as free text with no carbohydrate amount, so the twin forecasts forward as if the patient were fasting. The arm where we assumed a fixed 50 g per logged meal was *worse still* — meal information only helps when it is accurate, which matches what our own benchmark ablations predicted.
3. **Sampling is three times sparser than the twin expects.** These are 15-minute Libre traces; the particle filter was built around 5-minute CGM, so it updates a third as often and drifts in between.
4. **The observation-noise constant was chosen for our simulated sensor**, not for this one.

### What this does and does not change

It does not invalidate the design: the mechanistic core, the particle filter, the counterfactual rehearsal and the graceful-degradation ladder are unchanged, and the simulated results are reported exactly as before. What it does is put a number on the warning the README already carried — **the simulated results are an upper bound** — and show that the gap between simulation and reality is large rather than cosmetic.

We are reporting a failed external validation rather than omitting it. A reader can now see precisely how far this prototype is from clinical usefulness, which is more than most digital-twin papers make possible.

### What would have to happen next

* ~~Refit the EHR → physiology prior on real cohorts instead of on our own simulator.~~ **We tried this** — see `reports/PRIOR_REFIT.md`. It did not help. Refitting on real patients left the held-out result unchanged; the regression's residual spread exploded, which says the routine EHR fields barely predict these physiological parameters in a real cohort at all. Widening the prior and raising the assumed sensor noise moved the held-out ratio from 1.10 to 1.01 — parity with persistence, not better than it.
* Handle sparse and irregular sampling explicitly rather than upsampling to a 5-minute grid.
* Fit the observation-noise and process-noise constants per sensor.
* Then repeat this exact script and see whether the numbers move.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# download the dataset (CC BY 4.0) from https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.20444397
unzip data.zip -d shanghai/
python scripts/validate_shanghai.py shanghai/
```

The raw data are **not** redistributed in this repository. Citation: Zhao, Q., Zhu, J., Shen, X. et al. *Chinese diabetes datasets for data-driven machine learning.* Scientific Data 10, 35 (2023).
